In November 1985, Nevado del Ruiz, a volcano in the Colombian Andes, produced an eruption that was modest by the standards of volcanology. Yet it caused one of the deadliest volcanic disasters of the twentieth century. The summit was capped with glacial ice, and hot rock and gas thrown onto the ice melted part of it rapidly. The meltwater mixed with loose ash and soil on the steep slopes to form lahars, fast-moving flows of mud and debris. Channeled by river valleys, the lahars picked up more material as they descended and grew in volume.

About two and a half hours after the eruption began, a lahar reached the town of Armero, more than 40 kilometers from the summit. Most of the town was buried, and more than 20,000 of its residents died. The distance itself helps explain the toll. Lava rarely travels so far, and a town lying well beyond the reach of falling rock and hot gas could reasonably seem safe to the people who lived there.

The disaster was not entirely unforeseen. The volcano had shown signs of unrest for about a year, and a hazard map issued weeks before the eruption reportedly marked Armero as exposed to lahars. The warnings did not lead to an evacuation, however, partly because officials doubted the threat and partly because of confusion on the night itself. Many volcanologists have since argued that the disaster was less a failure of scientific prediction than of communication.

item.passage:
Water rises through a tall tree without any pump. According to the cohesion-tension theory, proposed by Henry Dixon and John Joly in 1894, evaporation from the leaves pulls on the water in the narrow conduits of the xylem, the plant's water-conducting tissue. Because water molecules cling strongly to one another, the pull is passed down an unbroken column to the roots. The water is therefore under tension, rather like a stretched rope, and the arrangement carries a risk: if the column breaks, it can no longer be pulled.

Such breaks, called embolisms, occur when an air bubble enters a conduit and expands to fill it. The bubble usually enters from a neighboring conduit that is already filled with air, slipping through the tiny pores in the wall between them. In the 1960s, researchers listening to drought-stressed plants with sensitive detectors reported faint clicks, which they interpreted as individual columns snapping. The drier the plant became, the more often the clicks came, since stronger tension draws air through the pores more easily.

Plants manage this risk rather than escape it. Many tolerate the loss of some conduits because water can be rerouted through others. Freezing poses a related danger, since air dissolved in the water forms bubbles when the water freezes, and wide conduits are more likely than narrow ones to stay blocked after a thaw. This may help explain why some trees of cold climates, such as many oaks, grow a new set of wide conduits each spring.

item.passage:
In seventeenth-century London, parish clerks compiled weekly Bills of Mortality, lists of burials and baptisms that had been issued, with interruptions, since the plague outbreaks of the previous century. The causes of death were reported by "searchers," usually elderly women without medical training who viewed each body. Most readers consulted the bills only to see whether plague was rising or falling. In 1662 John Graunt, a London haberdasher, published a short book that treated decades of these bills as data.

Graunt was frank about the records' flaws. He noticed, for example, that in plague years the deaths attributed to other causes also rose sharply, and he reasoned that some plague deaths had been recorded under other names, whether through error or to spare a household the quarantine imposed on the infected. Rather than discarding the bills, he adjusted for such distortions and looked for patterns that held across many years. He found that slightly more boys than girls were baptized, roughly fourteen to thirteen, and that this ratio was steady from year to year.

His estimates were rough, and some, including a table of how many people survived to each age, rested largely on guesswork. Historians nonetheless often treat the book as a founding work of demography because of its method: individual entries might be wrong, but large numbers of them, examined together, could still reveal regularities. Graunt was elected to the newly founded Royal Society, reportedly with the support of King Charles II.

item.passage:
In 1962 the linguist William Labov tested an idea about New York City speech. Many New Yorkers of the time sometimes pronounced the r sound after a vowel, as in "car," and sometimes dropped it, and Labov suspected that pronouncing it carried prestige. He chose three Manhattan department stores that served customers of different social standing: Saks Fifth Avenue at the top, Macy's in the middle, and S. Klein near the bottom. Since salespeople tend to borrow the speech of their customers, he reasoned, their pronunciation should vary by store.

Posing as a shopper, Labov asked employees where to find an item he knew was on the fourth floor. He then pretended not to have heard, so that they repeated "fourth floor" more carefully. The r sound was most frequent at Saks and least frequent at Klein, as predicted. The repetitions, however, revealed more. Employees at all three stores pronounced r more often when speaking carefully, but the increase was largest at Macy's, where many who dropped r at first produced it on repetition.

Labov read the jump at Macy's as a sign of insecurity: speakers in the middle seemed especially aware of the prestige form and reached for it when attention fell on their speech. The study was brief and crude by later standards, since Labov recorded each answer only in written notes and could not ask about the employees' backgrounds. Its larger contribution was to show that apparently random variation in speech can follow measurable social patterns.

item.passage:
In 1895 Wallace Sabine, a young physicist at Harvard, was asked to fix the lecture hall in the university's new Fogg Art Museum, where speech was hard to follow. The problem was reverberation: sound reflected from the hard walls and ceiling so persistently that each syllable was still audible while the next was being spoken. Sabine had no instruments suited to the task. He reportedly used an organ pipe as a steady source, a stopwatch, and his own ears, timing how long a tone took to fade to silence after the pipe stopped.

To vary the conditions, he and his assistants carried seat cushions from a nearby theater into the hall at night, adding them a few at a time and timing the decay after each addition. The results fit a simple rule. Reverberation time rose in proportion to the volume of the room and fell as the total absorption of its surfaces increased, so each cushion shortened it by a predictable amount. Sabine measured absorption in units equal to one square foot of open window, a surface that sends no sound back into the room.

The rule allowed a hall's reverberation to be calculated before the hall was built, and Sabine applied it as a consultant for Boston's Symphony Hall, which opened in 1900 and is still widely admired. His formula has limits, however. It assumes that sound is spread evenly through a room, and it predicts poorly where absorption is very heavy, cases for which later researchers proposed corrections.

After a wildfire, hillsides in dry regions such as southern California can shed rainwater as if they were paved. Part of the reason lies not at the surface but a few centimeters beneath it. Many plants, especially the shrubs of the chaparral, release waxy organic compounds into the soil, and even unburned soil under such vegetation may resist wetting to some degree. During a fire, heat vaporizes many of these compounds near the surface. Some of the vapor escapes into the air, but some is driven downward into cooler soil, where it condenses on the grains and coats them with a thin, water-repellent film.

The result, as the soil scientist Leonard DeBano and colleagues described in studies from the 1960s onward, is often a layered profile: a loose, wettable layer of ash and soil lying on top of a water-repellent one. When rain falls, the top layer soaks up water until it is saturated, but the layer below blocks further infiltration. Water then runs off across the slope, and the saturated top layer may slide with it, feeding the debris flows that sometimes follow fires.

More heat does not simply mean a worse problem, however. Laboratory heating suggests that repellency strengthens at moderate temperatures, roughly 175 to 270 degrees Celsius, but is largely destroyed above about 290 degrees. The most severely burned patches are therefore not necessarily the most repellent at the surface. The effect also usually weakens within a year or two as the coatings break down.

Western scrub-jays, birds of western North America, hide food in scattered caches and return to it days or weeks later. Other jays watch, and they steal. In an experiment published in 2001, Nathan Emery and Nicola Clayton at Cambridge let captive jays cache food in trays either while another jay looked on or while they were alone. Later, each bird was given its trays back in private. Birds that had been watched while caching moved many of their items to new sites that the observer had not seen; birds that had cached alone did so far less often.

The more striking result concerned which birds re-cached. Jays that had earlier had the chance to raid other birds' caches re-cached after being watched, but jays without that experience did not, although they too had been observed. Having been a thief, it seemed, changed how a bird guarded its own food. The researchers suggested that the birds might be drawing on their own past behavior to anticipate what an observer would do, a capacity sometimes called experience projection.

That interpretation remains debated. Critics have argued that a simpler mechanism could produce the same pattern: an association, formed during a bird's own raids, between an onlooker's presence and food going missing, with no representation of what another individual knows. Even so, the finding that protective behavior depended on a bird's history as a thief has made the scrub-jay a central case in discussions of whether animals other than primates can reason about other minds.

In the early 1620s, at the start of the Thirty Years' War, the German lands passed through a monetary crisis later called the Kipper- und Wipperzeit, a name usually linked to the tipping scales used to pick heavier coins out from lighter ones. The Holy Roman Empire had no single mint. Dozens of princes and cities held the right to strike coins, and the large silver taler was officially worth a fixed number of smaller coins such as the kreuzer.

Rulers short of money for soldiers could profit by striking small coins that contained less silver and more copper while keeping the same face value. Their agents exchanged the debased coins for good ones in neighboring territories, and the good coins were melted down to make still more bad ones. As confidence collapsed, the price of the taler in small coins rose steeply; in some cities it reportedly climbed from under 100 kreuzer to several hundred by 1622. Prices of bread and other goods followed.

The episode is sometimes called an early hyperinflation, but the label needs care. The large silver coins largely kept their value, so merchants who dealt in them were partly protected. The heaviest losses fell on people paid in small change, such as soldiers, laborers, and officials on fixed wages. Because the profits went to the issuers, the debasement worked as a hidden tax, and by about 1623 most authorities had returned to sounder coinage, partly because their own revenues were arriving in nearly worthless money.

Much of what historians know about the Roman army in Britain comes from inscriptions on stone, which record what soldiers and officers wished to make permanent. In 1973, however, excavators led by Robin Birley at Vindolanda, a fort near the later line of Hadrian's Wall, found something rarer: thin slivers of wood, roughly the size of a postcard, written on in ink. Most date from about 90 to 120 CE. They survived because the fort was repeatedly rebuilt, with fresh floors laid over older buildings, sealing damp layers of debris in which a lack of oxygen slowed decay.

The ink had often faded, and many texts could be read only in infrared photographs. Their contents are strikingly ordinary. One strength report states that a unit of more than 750 men had fewer than 300 present at the fort, the rest posted elsewhere or unfit. Other tablets request beer, mention deliveries of socks, or refer to local Britons by a dismissive nickname. A birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, the commander's wife, ends with lines thought to be in Claudia's own hand, among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman.

The tablets are not a balanced archive. They survive largely because they were thrown away, and some were apparently tossed onto a bonfire that went out before they burned. What remains is a scatter of discarded paperwork, weighted toward the commander's household. Yet that is precisely its value: documents no one meant to keep reveal routines that monuments omit.

In 1973, however, excavators led by Robin Birley at Vindolanda, a fort near the later line of Hadrian's Wall, found something rarer: thin slivers of wood, roughly the size of a postcard, written on in ink. Most date from about 90 to 120 CE. They survived because the fort was repeatedly rebuilt, with fresh floors laid over older buildings, sealing damp layers of debris in which a lack of oxygen slowed decay.

The ink had often faded, and many texts could be read only in infrared photographs. Their contents are strikingly ordinary. One strength report states that a unit of more than 750 men had fewer than 300 present at the fort, the rest posted elsewhere or unfit. Other tablets request beer, mention deliveries of socks, or refer to local Britons by a dismissive nickname. A birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, the commander's wife, ends with lines thought to be in Claudia's own hand, among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman.

The tablets are not a balanced archive. They survive largely because they were thrown away, and some were apparently tossed onto a bonfire that went out before they burned. What remains is a scatter of discarded paperwork, weighted toward the commander's household. Yet that is precisely its value: documents no one meant to keep reveal routines that monuments omit.

item.passage:
Viking crews sailed to Iceland and Greenland without the magnetic compass, which seems to have reached Europe only after the Viking Age. In clear weather they could steer by the Sun, but fog and overcast skies are common at those latitudes. In 1967 the Danish archaeologist Thorkild Ramskou proposed that they might have located the hidden Sun with a crystal. A medieval Icelandic saga describes King Olaf holding up a "sunstone" on a snowy day to find the Sun's position, and Ramskou suggested that the stone was Iceland spar, a clear form of calcite.

The idea rests on two physical facts. First, sunlight scattered in the sky is partly polarized, meaning its waves vibrate mainly in one direction, in a pattern arranged around the Sun's position. Second, Iceland spar splits light into two beams, so an object seen through it appears doubled, and the two images differ in brightness depending on how the crystal is turned relative to the light's polarization. By rotating the crystal until the two images look equally bright, a navigator could in principle infer the direction of the Sun even through cloud.

Experiments have since shown that people using calcite can locate the Sun within a few degrees under some conditions. Yet no sunstone has been recovered from any Viking site. The closest physical evidence is a calcite crystal found in the wreck of an English ship that sank near Alderney in 1592, lying close to its navigation instruments. The hypothesis is therefore plausible but unproven.

In 1925 the Chicago sociologist Ernest Burgess proposed that a growing city tends to arrange itself in rings around its center. At the core lay the central business district, in Chicago the Loop. Around it was a "zone in transition," where factories pressed into older housing and the newest and poorest immigrants usually settled. Beyond lay successive rings of working-class homes, middle-class residences, and, at the edge, a commuter zone. Burgess borrowed an idea from plant ecology: as the center expanded, each ring spread into the next, and groups that prospered moved outward, leaving their old neighborhoods to newcomers, a process he called succession.

The model was influential partly because it was simple and partly because it described movement rather than a fixed map. Critics soon noted its limits. In 1939 the land economist Homer Hoyt, after studying rents in many American cities, argued that high-rent areas tended to extend outward from the center in wedges, often along transport routes or high ground, rather than forming complete rings. In 1945 the geographers Chauncy Harris and Edward Ullman went further, arguing that large cities grow around several centers, such as ports and industrial districts, instead of one.

The pattern also fails outside its setting. In many Latin American and European cities, wealthy households have long favored central districts, while poorer residents occupy the edges. Burgess's rings fit a fast-growing industrial city with cheap transport outward; a model can capture a real process and still be tied to one place and time.
